narrative.text: The title page of Web Annex B (evidence synthesis and analysis) to WHO's consolidated tuberculosis guidelines, Module 3: Diagnosis.

The copyright and cataloguing page, with Creative Commons licence terms, noting that the annex supports the TB diagnosis guideline and is published for transparency. It also lists the usual WHO disclaimers on third-party materials and liability.

The first page of the table of contents, listing web annexes B.1 onwards that cover reviews of low complexity automated NAATs, other diagnostic tests and qualitative syntheses on targeted next-generation sequencing.
The final page of the table of contents, listing annexes B.20 to B.23 on the accuracy, safety, cost-effectiveness and economic modelling of TB antigen-based skin tests.
A brief acknowledgement thanking the experts who carried out the systematic reviews in the web annex.

The title, author list and affiliations for Web Annex B.1, a systematic review of how accurately low complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (LC-aNAATs) detect pulmonary TB and isoniazid or rifampicin resistance in adults and adolescents.

Gives background for the LC-aNAAT review, citing 2022 global estimates of TB incidence and rifampicin-resistant TB and WHO's recommendation of rapid molecular tests as initial diagnostics. It explains WHO's grouping of tests into classes and the clinical importance of detecting rifampicin and isoniazid resistance.

Lists the index tests in the LC-aNAAT class and describes the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and Truenat assays, including how they detect TB, report semi-quantitative results and target the rpoB gene for rifampicin resistance.
Describes the STANDARD M10 molecular system and its TB assays, then outlines the review's methods, including literature searches carried out in October 2023 across several databases.

Lists further sources searched for the LC-aNAAT review, including trial registries, dissertations and a WHO public call for data, and sets out eligibility criteria. It introduces the two reference standards used, culture and a composite reference standard.

Defines the culture and composite reference standards, then describes data extraction, quality assessment with QUADAS-2 and planned meta-analyses of sensitivity and specificity by subgroup such as smear and HIV status.
Explains the class pooling criteria and bivariate meta-analysis models used for the LC-aNAAT review, then reports search results for Xpert Ultra, yielding 33 included studies.
A caption for the study flow diagram for Xpert Ultra.
Reports search results for the Truenat assays, with five reports included in the review, and captions the corresponding study flow diagram.

Reports that no eligible studies were found for STANDARD M10 or other new LC-aNAATs and summarizes the 36 included studies, mostly of Xpert Ultra, with eleven assessing rifampicin resistance detection.
Describes the respiratory specimen types used in the included studies, mainly sputum, with some using bronchoalveolar lavage or pooled samples.
The first page of Table 1, giving characteristics of the Xpert Ultra studies, such as reference standard, design, share of people with HIV, setting, age group, country and specimen type.
Continues Table 1 of Xpert Ultra study characteristics, covering further studies from South Africa, Malawi, Switzerland, China and elsewhere.
Ends Table 1 of Xpert Ultra study characteristics, with abbreviations for culture media and other terms.
Table 2, giving characteristics of the Truenat studies, conducted mainly in India and several African and Asia-Pacific countries, including rates of non-determinate results.
Summarizes the risk of bias and applicability assessment for the included LC-aNAAT studies, listing those judged high risk or of concern and why.
A caption for the summary figure of risk of bias and applicability across studies of respiratory specimens.

Begins the findings of the LC-aNAAT review, introducing Table 3 of summary sensitivity and specificity estimates for the class and individual tests. The table rows cover analyses by reference standard, specimen and smear status.

Continues Table 3 of LC-aNAAT diagnostic accuracy, giving pooled sensitivity, specificity and predictive values by history of TB, age group, HIV status and for rifampicin resistance. Predictive values are calculated at an assumed 10% pre-test probability.
Gives footnotes to the accuracy table explaining the statistical models used, then discusses studies with lower sensitivity. One example is a Malawi trial enrolling only people with HIV.
Discusses studies with lower specificity, such as those enrolling people previously treated for TB, and introduces the analysis against a composite reference standard, done only for Xpert Ultra.
A blank page with no extracted text.
Table 4, listing the composite reference standard definitions used in each Xpert Ultra study, with a caption for the related risk-of-bias figure.

Reports that against a composite reference standard, LC-aNAATs had a summary sensitivity of about 70% and specificity of about 99%, with illustrative numbers per 1000 people tested. It then introduces the analysis for people living with HIV.
Summarizes the twelve studies of sputum testing in people living with HIV, giving the range of sensitivities and specificities, with captions for the related figures.
Introduces the analysis of LC-aNAATs in HIV-negative adults and adolescents and then describes the frequency of Xpert Ultra trace results across studies.
Reports how classifying Xpert Ultra trace results as positive or negative changes pooled sensitivity and specificity, and introduces the rifampicin resistance analysis.
Reports a pooled sensitivity of about 95% and specificity of about 98% for LC-aNAAT detection of rifampicin resistance, with evidence graded high certainty.

Notes that no eligible studies assessed rifampicin resistance detection in people living with HIV, then begins the review's discussion and main conclusions, including the effect of how trace results are interpreted.
Concludes the main findings on LC-aNAAT accuracy for TB and rifampicin resistance, discusses strengths, limitations and implications, and states authors' contributions.
The start of the reference list of included Xpert Ultra studies for the LC-aNAAT review.
Continues the reference list of included Xpert Ultra studies, citing diagnostic accuracy studies from various countries.
Ends the Xpert Ultra references and lists included Truenat studies, among them an unpublished South African evaluation.
Appendix 1, giving the detailed MEDLINE search strategy for the LC-aNAAT review.
Continues the search strategies, covering MEDLINE terms for the index tests and searches in Web of Science and Scopus.
Gives the search strategies used in the Cochrane Central Register and ProQuest dissertations.
Appendix 2, summary of findings tables for LC-aNAATs in diagnosing pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance, giving pooled accuracy and certainty of evidence.
Ends a summary of findings table with expected true and false results per 1,000 people tested at several prevalences, graded high certainty.
Introduces Appendix 3, additional forest plots of LC-aNAATs by brand and subgroup, and explains how head-to-head studies were handled to avoid double counting.
Captions for forest plots of LC-aNAAT accuracy by brand among people living with HIV and HIV-negative people.
Captions for forest plots of LC-aNAAT accuracy by brand in smear-positive and smear-negative people.
Captions for forest plots of LC-aNAAT accuracy by brand in people with and without a history of TB.
Captions for forest plots of rifampicin resistance detection by brand and of Xpert Ultra accuracy in adolescents.
Captions for forest plots of LC-aNAAT accuracy in adults and of rifampicin resistance detection by smear status.

Appendix 4, a table of Xpert Ultra trace results per study and the share that were true positives, with summary estimates when trace results are treated as negative. The page ends with the title of the next annex, B.2.

The title, author list and affiliations for Web Annex B.2, a systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of low complexity automated NAATs for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in children.

Gives background on the paediatric TB burden, citing 2022 estimates of cases and deaths among children under 15, and the challenges of diagnosing TB in children. It then begins the methods, listing the databases searched in October 2023.

Completes the search methods of the paediatric LC-aNAAT review, including trial registries, reference lists and dissertations, and describes study selection, data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment. It also explains the meta-analysis approach and the use of GRADE to rate certainty separately for sensitivity and specificity.

Reports that 23 studies evaluated Xpert Ultra in children using sputum, gastric aspirate, nasopharyngeal aspirate, stool or extrapulmonary specimens, and summarizes their settings and reference standards.
The first page of Table 1, listing key characteristics of included paediatric Xpert Ultra studies, such as country, TB burden, setting, specimen type, design and reference standard.
Completes the table of paediatric study characteristics and summarizes the risk of bias and applicability judgements for studies using sputum specimens.
Summarizes risk-of-bias and applicability judgements for paediatric Xpert Ultra studies using sputum, gastric aspirate and stool specimens, domain by domain.

Completes the quality assessment for stool and other specimens, then begins a table of summary diagnostic accuracy of Xpert Ultra in children by specimen type and reference standard. The table rows cover sputum and gastric aspirate against culture or a composite standard.
Continues the paediatric accuracy table for nasopharyngeal aspirate and stool, then begins reporting results for sputum against culture, with eleven studies meta-analysed.

Reports that Xpert Ultra on children's sputum had a summary sensitivity of about 75% and specificity of about 96% against culture, with high-certainty evidence and illustrative figures per 1,000 children.
Reports a much lower summary sensitivity of about 24% for Xpert Ultra on children's sputum against a composite reference standard, with specificity of 100%.
Introduces the analysis of Xpert Ultra on sputum in children living with HIV against culture, with illustrative numbers of true and false results per 1,000 children.
Reports that, against a composite reference standard, Xpert Ultra on sputum from children living with HIV had a summary sensitivity of about 19% and specificity of 100%.
Gives illustrative results per 1,000 children living with HIV against the composite standard and introduces the analysis of gastric aspirate specimens.
Reports a summary sensitivity of about 70% and specificity of about 91% for Xpert Ultra on gastric aspirate against culture in children, with moderate-certainty evidence.
Reports a summary sensitivity of about 49% and specificity of about 99% for Xpert Ultra on gastric aspirate against a composite reference standard in children.
Reports that Xpert Ultra on nasopharyngeal aspirate had a summary sensitivity of about 46% against culture in children, with illustrative numbers per 1,000 tested.
Reports low sensitivity for Xpert Ultra on nasopharyngeal aspirate against a composite reference standard and introduces the analysis of stool specimens against culture.
Reports a summary sensitivity of about 68% and specificity of about 98% for Xpert Ultra on stool in children against a microbiological reference standard.
Introduces the analysis of Xpert Ultra on stool against a composite reference standard, with illustrative numbers of true and false results per 1,000 children.
Describes subgroup analyses by HIV status, age and nutritional status and reports sparse data on Xpert Ultra detection of rifampicin resistance in children's sputum.
Begins the results on extrapulmonary TB in children, reporting on Xpert Ultra accuracy in cerebrospinal fluid for tuberculous meningitis against culture.
Reports two small studies of Xpert Ultra on cerebrospinal fluid against a composite reference standard, with low sensitivity, and introduces the lymph node analysis.
Reports two small studies of Xpert Ultra on lymph node tissue and aspirates against culture, with high sensitivity and variable specificity; no meta-analysis was performed.

Reports small studies of Xpert Ultra on lymph node specimens against a composite reference standard and on other extrapulmonary specimens, too few for meta-analysis. The text contains a typographical error in the sensitivity range.

Summarizes the main results of the paediatric review, giving Xpert Ultra sensitivity and specificity by specimen type and reference standard. It notes that sensitivity was similar for sputum, gastric aspirate and stool.
Concludes that Xpert Ultra specificity exceeded 90% for each specimen type, though formal comparisons were not made, then gives acknowledgements and begins the list of included study references.
Continues the references of included paediatric Xpert Ultra studies.
Ends the included study references and begins the list of excluded studies, each with its reason for exclusion.
Continues the list of excluded studies, citing reasons such as adult populations, inability to separate data for children under 10, or unpublished data.
Continues the excluded studies list with reasons, including registered trials whose data were unpublished or incomplete.
Continues the excluded studies list, including TB-Speed trials and studies not designed to assess diagnostic accuracy.
Continues the excluded studies list, mostly studies that could not separate data for young children or enrolled adults.
Continues the excluded studies list with reasons for each exclusion.
Ends the excluded studies list and begins the other references, citing GRADE guidance on certainty of test accuracy evidence.
Ends the other references, citing GRADE guidance and WHO consolidated guidelines and handbooks on TB diagnosis.
Appendix 1, the MEDLINE search strategy for the paediatric LC-aNAAT review, combining TB, child and test name terms.
Gives the Embase and Web of Science search strategies for the paediatric review.
Gives the Web of Science, Scopus and regional database search strategies for the paediatric review.
Gives the Cochrane library and trial registry search strategies for the paediatric review.
Appendix 2, PRISMA diagram captions for Truenat and for STANDARD M10 and IRON-qPCR in the paediatric review.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Appendix 3, the start of a table of Xpert Ultra subgroup accuracy for paediatric pulmonary TB by HIV status, age group and specimen type. It also covers reference standard, giving pooled sensitivity, specificity and predictive values.
Continues the subgroup accuracy table for children aged 1–4 years and other subgroups by specimen and reference standard.
Ends the subgroup accuracy table with nasopharyngeal aspirate and stool results and abbreviations; some confidence intervals in the stool row appear misprinted in the source.
The title, authors and affiliations of Web Annex B.3, a systematic review of LC-aNAAT accuracy for extrapulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in adults and adolescents.

Gives background on extrapulmonary TB, which made up a fifth of notified TB cases in 2022, and on rifampicin-resistant TB. It describes Xpert Ultra's improved detection limit compared with Xpert MTB/RIF and its new trace result category.
Explains how Xpert Ultra trace results should be interpreted and describes the other index tests, including Truenat, STANDARD M10 and the multiplex IRON-qPCR platform.
Describes the IRON-qPCR kit for detecting TB and resistance to many drugs, then sets out the review's methods for analysing results per participant and by type of extrapulmonary TB.
Explains the meta-analysis approach for the extrapulmonary review, including bivariate models and analyses by reference standard, and introduces the search results.
A continuation of the Drummond checklist for further novel skin test studies, covering incremental and sensitivity analyses and the basis of conclusions.
The last Drummond checklist items for further novel skin test studies, on comparison with other work, generalisability and implementation.
Table A8 begins applying the Drummond checklist to economic studies of the tuberculin skin test and IGRA, for five studies from 2011–2012.
A continuation of Table A8, covering effectiveness evidence and the range of costs and consequences for the first five tuberculin skin test and IGRA studies.
A continuation of Table A8, covering which cost components were included and how costs were valued.
A continuation of Table A8, covering valuation of consequences, discounting and incremental analysis.
A continuation of Table A8, covering allowance for uncertainty and the basis of study conclusions.
A continuation of Table A8, covering comparison with other studies, generalisability and implementation issues.
A continuation of Table A8 for five studies from 2013, covering study questions, alternatives and effectiveness.
A continuation of the Drummond checklist for the 2013 studies, covering effectiveness evidence and the range of costs and consequences.
The study flow diagram for the extrapulmonary LC-aNAAT review, showing records identified, screened, excluded and included, with a PRISMA reference.
A continuation of the Drummond checklist for the 2013 studies, covering cost components and the sources of values.
A continuation of the Drummond checklist for the 2013 studies, covering market values, discounting and the discount rate used.
A continuation of the Drummond checklist for the 2013 studies, covering incremental analysis and sensitivity of results to key parameters.
A continuation of the Drummond checklist for the 2013 studies, covering how conclusions were reached and other factors considered.
The final Drummond checklist item for the 2013 studies, on discussion of implementation feasibility.
A near-blank page carrying only a page number and the heading for a continuation of Table A8.

Begins a table applying the Drummond checklist for economic evaluations to five cost-effectiveness studies of tuberculosis infection testing published in 2015–2017. All five compared costs and effects of alternatives for groups such as people with HIV, refugees, immigrants and people entering jail, and most included a do-nothing option.

Continues the Drummond checklist table for the same five studies, on how effectiveness was established. None used randomized trials; most drew test sensitivity and specificity from clinical studies or reviews, and the table notes how well their assumptions were referenced.

Continues the checklist table on whether the studies identified and measured all relevant costs and consequences. It records gaps such as unclear cost breakdowns, missing capital costs and one study omitting treatment and outcome costs.
Continues the checklist on valuation and discounting, noting that future costs were mostly discounted at 1.5–3.5% with rates justified by national guidance, while one study did not discount.

Table 1 of a systematic review on low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (LC-aNAATs) for extrapulmonary TB, listing included Xpert Ultra studies by country, reference standard, share of people with HIV, setting and specimen type. Most studies are from tertiary centres in high-burden countries such as South Africa, Uganda and India.
Records that all five studies did incremental analyses and allowed for uncertainty, with only one finding its results sensitive to the treatments received.
Records whether each study reported cost-effectiveness ratios, compared results with other work, and discussed generalizability and other decision factors.
Records whether each study discussed implementation issues such as feasibility and redeployment of freed resources.
A page marking the continuation of Table A8.

Applies the Drummond checklist to a second set of five cost-effectiveness studies of tuberculosis infection testing from 2017–2018. Their target groups include young immigrants to Norway, health workers, US-born people and migrants, recent UK immigrants and elderly care home residents in Hong Kong.

Shows how the second set of studies established effectiveness, mainly from clinical studies of test accuracy, and notes key assumptions such as no quality-of-life loss from uncomplicated treatment. It also records that all covered a wide enough range of costs and viewpoints.

Records for the second set of studies whether capital and operating costs were included and whether any items were left out of measurement. Notes include unclear hospital cost breakdowns and omitted costs that may underestimate totals.
Records discount rates of 3–5% and their justification for the second set of studies, all of which performed incremental analyses.

Records statistical and sensitivity analyses for the second set of studies, noting results sensitive to IGRA cost, infection rate and TST sensitivity, and whether results were compared with other studies.
Records whether the second set of studies discussed generalizability, other decision factors and implementation.

Continues Table 1 of included studies, adding studies from Colombia, Spain, Uganda, China and India with their reference standards and specimen types. Footnotes define the culture methods and abbreviations.
A page marking the continuation of Table A8.

Applies the Drummond checklist to a third set of five studies from 2018–2019, covering adolescent contacts in Japan, immigrants to Canada, migrants with kidney disease, and health workers in Brazil and Singapore. All compared costs and effects of alternatives, and none used randomized trials.

Shows how the third set of studies established effectiveness from clinical studies and reviews and comments on their key assumptions. One study assumed perfect test accuracy, while another gave no references for its assumptions.

Records cost coverage for the third set of studies, such as whether overheads and equipment were included. It also notes omitted items judged to have minimal impact and whether value sources were stated.
Records discounting choices for the third set of studies, with some not discounting because of short time horizons, and confirms that all did incremental analyses.
Records sensitivity analyses for the third set of studies, including sensitivity to QFT-GIT cost and to migrants' origin, and whether conclusions used cost-effectiveness ratios.
Records whether the third set of studies compared results with others and discussed generalizability, decision factors and implementation.
A page containing only a page number.
A page marking the continuation of Table A8.

Applies the Drummond checklist to a final four studies from 2018–2020, covering recent immigrants in Oman, a general population, adults with HIV in Brazil and pregnant women with HIV. None included a do-nothing option or used trials, and all drew test accuracy from reviews or clinical studies.

Reports that 36 Xpert Ultra studies and three Truenat MTB Plus studies were included, with no eligible studies for other index tests, so pooled estimates come from Xpert Ultra only. It notes that GRADE summary of findings tables are in an appendix and presents a risk of bias and applicability summary figure.

Records the effectiveness assumptions of the final four studies, noting one that imputed rates from Omani data without clear assumptions. It also records how fully each covered costs, including overheads and equipment.
Records how credibly the final four studies valued costs and how they discounted, with one study lacking clear value sources, market values and discounting. All performed incremental analyses.
Records sensitivity results for the final four studies, such as sensitivity to QFT-GIT specificity, DiaskinTest cost and TB risk, and whether they discussed generalizability and other factors.
Records whether the final four studies discussed implementation issues.
The title of Table A9, summarizing the proportion of articles meeting each Drummond criterion.

Table A9 gives the share of all reviewed economic studies, DiaskinTest studies and TST or IGRA studies meeting each Drummond criterion. Almost all compared alternatives and drew effectiveness from clinical studies, none used randomized trials, and few included capital costs, while 60% discounted future costs.

Continues Table A9 with the share of reviewed studies meeting the remaining Drummond criteria, from discount rate justification to discussion of implementation. DiaskinTest-related studies met many criteria less often than TST or IGRA studies, for example in sensitivity analysis and comparison with other work.
A blank page with no extracted text.

The title page of Web Annex B.23, a modelling study of the economic evidence for tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests, naming the review team and stating it was prepared for a February 2022 WHO guideline meeting.
A list of abbreviations used in the economic modelling annex on tuberculosis skin tests.

Table 2 gives pooled sensitivity, specificity and predictive values of LC-aNAATs for extrapulmonary TB by specimen and reference standard, with cerebrospinal fluid showing 88.2% sensitivity against microbiological reference. Pleural fluid and urine show lower sensitivity against a composite reference standard.

The extended summary explains that a Markov model was built to compare the cost-effectiveness of new antigen-based skin tests with the PPD tuberculin skin test and IGRA in Brazil, South Africa and the UK, focusing on DiaskinTest because only its maker supplied costs. Costs are from a health system perspective, and sensitivity analyses explore test prices and uncertainty in clinical and utility parameters.

Reports that DiaskinTest was cost saving with small QALY gains against both comparators in Brazil and South Africa, and against the skin test but not IGRA in the UK, where it remained cost-effective, and sets out how far test prices could rise and stay cost saving. The interpretation stresses that results depend on country-specific costing and limited evidence and that other new skin tests could not be modelled for lack of cost data.
Concludes that since accuracy appears similar across new skin tests, unit cost will mainly drive cost-effectiveness, which may vary by country.

States the research question and objectives of the modelling: comparing antigen-based skin tests with IGRA and PPD skin tests in Brazil, South Africa and the UK using a Markov model and sensitivity analyses. The outcomes are cost-effectiveness ratios or net benefit per QALY and test costs per patient.
Explains that the economic report has two parts and that this document is Section B, with Section A submitted separately.

Describes the Markov model, which follows a cohort without active TB through testing for infection, treatment, completion or interruption, active TB, recovery or death, across eleven states. It is parametrized for the UK, Brazil and South Africa, and the modelling objectives are restated.

Describes the model diagram and parameters, starting with 100,000 people tested and followed over 20 annual cycles. Test accuracy comes from the authors' systematic review, the skin test's specificity is assumed equal to IGRA's, and the model covers the general population without separating by HIV status.

Table 1 lists model parameters by country, including the prevalence of TB infection, treatment initiation, completion and interruption, progression to active TB, treatment efficacy, TB treatment coverage and recovery rates.

Continues the parameters with TB death rates and the sensitivity and specificity of the skin tests and IGRA. It explains that DiaskinTest unit costs combine the manufacturer's price with standard skin test costs, and that the largest observed country costs were chosen as a conservative assumption.

Describes how testing and treatment costs were drawn from published studies for each country, and explains the QALY assumptions, 20-year horizon and country discount rates. It lists the sensitivity and scenario analyses, including a worst case in which one vial is used for a single patient.

Completes Table 2 with estimates for urine, bone or joint fluid, pericardial, peritoneal and blood specimens, where bone or joint fluid shows high sensitivity. It then introduces the results for tuberculous meningitis.

Gives the extra cost of the single-use vial scenario and describes the three testing strategies compared, with results reported as cost-effectiveness ratios or net benefit against country thresholds. Table 2 lists unit costs of each test by country and utility values.
Completes the utility values and notes on test costs, then gives Table 3 on the cost of TB infection treatment regimens by country. Costs are shown as drug and staff costs in 2021 US dollars.

Table 4 gives the costs of treating drug-sensitive active TB under directly observed therapy in each country, with notes on visit and test costs. The results section begins with Brazil, where DiaskinTest was cost saving compared with both other tests.

Completes the Brazil results, showing that any antigen skin test would stay cost saving against the PPD skin test up to about three times DiaskinTest's price. In the worst-case vial scenario it would no longer save costs but would remain cost-effective.

Presents cost-effectiveness planes and results for South Africa, where DiaskinTest was cost saving against both comparators and would remain so up to a modestly higher price. In the worst-case vial scenario it would remain cost-effective, and the UK results begin.

Reports UK results, where DiaskinTest was cost saving compared with the skin test and cost-effective compared with IGRA, staying cost-effective at prices up to about 2.35 times its own cost. Table 5 sets out modelled costs, QALYs and incremental net benefit for each strategy in the three countries.

Interprets the results, noting that DiaskinTest dominated the other tests in Brazil and South Africa but cost more than IGRA in the UK. It discusses limits such as manufacturer costs that vary with order size, wasted doses from opened vials, the provider-only perspective and differences between study and real-world costing.

Explains that unit costs vary widely between countries because of different costing methods and assumptions about clinic visits, and that other new skin tests could not be modelled because they are not yet marketed. It suggests future work on at-risk groups such as people with HIV, children, contacts and migrants.
The first part of the reference list for the economic modelling annex, citing studies on latent TB burden, cascades of care, test accuracy and cost-effectiveness.
Completes the reference list, citing cost-effectiveness and treatment cost studies from Brazil, South Africa and the UK and WHO TB treatment guidance.

Reports that Xpert Ultra on cerebrospinal fluid had 88.2% sensitivity and 96.0% specificity against a microbiological reference and 60.3% sensitivity against a composite reference for tuberculous meningitis.
Supplementary tables give the calculated prevalence of TB infection in Brazil, the UK and South Africa and estimated rates of progression from infection to active TB.
Gives progression rates for people with HIV and explains that the model could be adapted for such groups. Table B3 shows uninflated TB infection treatment costs by regimen and country.

Explains how treatment staff costs were calculated, then Tables B4 and B5 give DiaskinTest vial prices by order volume and delivery costs by country. They work these out as a cost per patient, using manufacturer data.
Applies the Drummond checklist to the authors' own modelling study, which compared alternatives and drew test accuracy from clinical studies and reviews.
Continues the self-assessment, noting that diagnostic, treatment, staff and laboratory costs were included and that costs were discounted with justification.
Completes the self-assessment, reporting appropriate statistical and sensitivity analyses and discussion of generalizability and implementation.
The title page of Web Annex F, a review of qualitative evidence on tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests, naming the review team prepared for the February 2022 WHO guideline meeting.
A page containing only a stray character.

Lists abbreviations and opens the executive summary, explaining that end-user values, acceptability, feasibility and equity effects of new TB skin tests are unknown. It describes three work packages: systematic reviews of qualitative evidence, 20 interviews with providers and people with TB infection, and an online discrete choice experiment. Confidence in evidence was rated with GRADE-CERQual.

Reports that the reviews found only four relevant studies, of low to moderate confidence, while the interviews covered 20 people and the choice experiment 234 respondents, mainly from India, the United States and South Africa. Providers and consumers valued accuracy, convenience, a positive experience, low cost and low resource needs. They preferred tests that avoid follow-up visits and specialist staff and use existing infrastructure.
A figure caption for forest plots of LC-aNAAT accuracy in cerebrospinal fluid, followed by an introduction to results for lymph node TB.

Reports that new skin tests were seen as more accurate than the tuberculin skin test but sharing its drawbacks compared with IGRA, which remained preferred where already in use. They appear feasible and low-cost where the tuberculin skin test is already used and are unlikely to create new equity problems. The conclusion finds them more acceptable than and as feasible as the tuberculin skin test, with likely equity benefits.

Sets out the background to a study of end-user values and preferences on tests for TB infection, comparing the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA). It notes that IGRAs are preferred in high-income settings partly because they need only one visit. It then explains that IGRAs cost more and need laboratories, phlebotomy and trained technicians, and are often run in batches.

Describes the drawbacks of IGRAs and introduces newer TB antigen-based skin tests (TBST) such as C-Tb, Diaskintest and the ESAT6-CFP10 test, which may match IGRA accuracy at lower cost. It then states the project's aim of exploring end-user preferences and trade-offs through a systematic review, interviews and a discrete choice experiment.

Lists the three work packages of the TB skin test preference study (qualitative evidence review, end-user interviews and a discrete choice experiment) and notes the role of a multidisciplinary expert advisory panel.

Introduces the first work package, two systematic reviews of qualitative evidence on end-user views of antigen-based skin tests compared with IGRA and TST, and their possible equity effects. It describes the databases searched, including Russian and Chinese sources, plus manual searches and a WHO public call for data.

Sets out the eligibility criteria for the qualitative reviews, which included studies using qualitative data collection and analysis and excluded those analysing qualitative data quantitatively. It also covers the populations, tests and settings considered and how two reviewers screened the results in several languages.

Describes how qualitative data on acceptability, feasibility and equity, plus study characteristics, were extracted in duplicate. It explains the thematic synthesis approach and the use of GRADE-CERQual to judge confidence in each review finding.
Reports that four studies met inclusion criteria: one on the Diaskintest from a WHO call for data and three on IGRA and TST, published between 2014 and 2021, with PRISMA flow charts.

Describes the four included studies, from a mass child screening programme in Russia's Penza region to HIV clinic services and immigrant screening in the Netherlands. It summarises their methodological limitations, such as missing participant quotes and unreported ethics. It begins the GRADE-CERQual assessment of confidence in the findings.

Reports moderate confidence in the review findings on values, acceptability and feasibility and low confidence for health equity, citing small numbers of studies, thin data and focus on narrow subgroups.

Reports pooled Xpert Ultra accuracy on lymph node aspirate, with 85.3% sensitivity and 74.1% specificity against a microbiological reference and 71.3% sensitivity against a composite reference, with low to very low certainty.

A table of characteristics of the four studies included in the qualitative reviews, covering test type, country, setting, participants, data collection, analysis, frameworks and conflicts of interest.

Introduces the combined qualitative findings on test values, acceptability, feasibility and equity, noting how limited the data were. It reports that accuracy shaped preferences, with IGRA often favoured over TST for being less subjective, although some clinic staff doubted IGRA accuracy in people with HIV.

Reports how convenience factors such as clinic waits, transport and crowding affected preferences for IGRA and TST, while the Diaskintest was seen as convenient for mass screening. It then discusses people-related factors in test acceptability, including discomfort from the TST, illustrated with quotes from South Africa.

Describes test-related factors affecting acceptability, with TBST and IGRA seen as more specific than TST and the Diaskintest's specificity encouraging parents to test their children. It notes no contextual factors affected acceptability. It then opens the feasibility findings, which came only from IGRA and TST studies and were rated with moderate confidence.

Explains that the need for a second clinic visit to read the TST was a key feasibility concern, especially where travel and waiting times are long, while IGRA needs only one visit. It reports provider views from South Africa that using routine blood draws could ease follow-up problems, along with a patient's worry about delays.

Continues the feasibility findings with concerns about infrequent blood draws delaying detection, and notes that public funding and supply of the TST helped feasibility in South Africa. It then summarises health equity issues, including access and transport barriers, staffing, scalability for mass screening and suitability for children, people with HIV and needle-phobic people.

Expands on equity issues, highlighting the return visit for TST reading as a barrier and shortages of trained staff for TST and IGRA. It notes the Diaskintest was reported as suitable for mass screening of children, while some US clinicians doubted IGRA results in people with HIV.

Summarises the systematic review findings: data on antigen-based skin tests were scarce and setting-specific, and key values included accuracy, convenience, patient experience, cost and resources. It explains how these findings shaped the interview guide and discrete choice experiment.

Introduces the second work package, qualitative interviews with 20 people with TB and providers recruited through global networks and organisations such as TB civil society groups and the Stop TB Partnership. It describes the email invitation and the interview topics, tailored to consumers and providers.

Lists the interview topics, from current skin test use to preferences, feasibility, acceptability and equity, and explains that interviews were transcribed and coded in NVivo. A table and figure describe the 13 providers and 7 consumers from high- and low/middle-income countries.
A figure caption for lymph node aspirate forest plots, introducing results for lymph node tissue.

Explains that the interview analysis reused the people, test and contextual factor framework from the review. It reports that participants valued accuracy and saw TBST and IGRA as more accurate than TST, with downstream benefits such as avoiding unnecessary treatment and stress.

Reports interviewees' concerns that false-positive TST results cause costly and stressful follow-up. It describes how IGRA was seen as more convenient because it needs one visit. It also notes that IGRAs demand more resources, such as laboratories, phlebotomy and trained staff, than skin tests.

Notes a provider's view that TBSTs need little laboratory infrastructure. It then presents people-related factors in acceptability, such as consumer experience and perceptions of skin tests, with mixed views on whether new tests would cause anxiety.

Presents interview quotes on fears about skin test injections and live readings, and on blood draws as a barrier to IGRA, including cultural beliefs about blood. It shows that initial worries about injections often eased with experience. It also contrasts the invasiveness of skin and blood tests.

Reports that the complexity of skin test procedures may reduce acceptability among people with low health literacy. It discusses demographic concerns about using IGRA and TBST in some groups. It also includes providers' hopes for less invasive formats and one view that skin testing should be abandoned altogether.

Continues with participants' views that skin tests are outdated technology and that most knew little about TBST, calling for public awareness and evidence. It reports that clear explanation and endorsement by providers and WHO were expected to improve acceptability.

Reports that some consumers doubted the usefulness of TBST without evidence that it beats existing tests, or questioned what care follows a positive result. Providers expected the new skin tests to match IGRA specificity in skin-test form and would prefer them over the TST.

Presents provider criticism of how subjective TST readings are and lists perceived benefits of TBST's greater accuracy, including use in people who inject drugs. It also notes that none of the tests can distinguish latent from active TB.

Reports views on the difficulty of developing a biomarker that separates latent from active TB. It describes contextual factors in acceptability, such as provider perceptions and follow-up infrastructure, including consequences like deportation after positive tests in travellers. It notes that hospital settings caused anxiety for some consumers.

Opens the interview findings on feasibility, noting that consumer experience was the only people factor raised. It reports that IGRA's single-visit requirement was seen as a clear advantage that lets providers focus follow-up on positive cases.
Reports pooled Xpert Ultra accuracy on lymph node tissue, with 96.5% sensitivity and 79.4% specificity against a microbiological reference and lower sensitivity against a composite reference.

Presents quotes on the single-visit benefit of IGRA versus repeat TST visits and on transport burdens, especially in lower-income countries. It introduces four test factors affecting feasibility: cost, time to result, portability and ease of administration, starting with the lower cost of skin tests.

Reports providers' views that the lower cost of TBST could save money and make government funding more likely, including for testing children. It discusses time to result and the portability of skin tests for community outreach. It notes that the TST was considered fairly easy to administer with trained staff.

Presents quotes on the TST technique being fiddly at first but manageable with training, and on the need for frequent retraining in community settings. It also includes a wish for simpler tests such as fingerprick assays. It then introduces contextual factors in feasibility: resource needs, the COVID-19 pandemic and the health system setting.

Describes contextual factors affecting the feasibility of tests for TB infection, noting that skin tests (TBST and TST) and IGRA all need trained staff and equipment, while IGRA also needs a laboratory, a blood draw and travel to a facility. It introduces equity factors, with tests needing less infrastructure seen as more accessible in resource-limited settings.

Discusses how tests for TB infection affect health equity, explaining that skin tests are more portable and may not need a facility visit, which helps people living far from clinics. It notes that IGRA was seen as less suited to low-income settings because of its cost and resource needs.

Presents interview quotes on affordability and the value of simple skin tests where phlebotomy is unavailable, and notes that skin tests may suit groups in whom finding veins is hard. It concludes that equity effects of these tests may differ by population.

Summarizes the user interview findings: providers and consumers valued accuracy, convenience, a good patient experience, low cost and low resource needs. The new antigen-based skin tests were seen as matching IGRA accuracy at lower cost and resource needs, and as more accurate than the TST at similar cost. Interviewees cautioned that in low-income settings the TBST alone would not fix wider access barriers such as stock, staff training and equipment.

Concludes that antigen-based skin tests were judged more acceptable than and as feasible as the TST, with equity benefits, and possibly preferable in resource-limited settings, while IGRA remains favoured in high-income countries; these findings shaped the discrete choice experiment.

Introduces Work Package C, a discrete choice experiment to measure the trade-offs consumers and providers are willing to make between attributes of TB infection tests. It explains how attributes were drawn from the reviews and interviews, covering acceptability, accuracy, feasibility and health equity.

Explains how the choice tasks were built, each offering two hypothetical tests plus an opt-out, with separate versions for providers and consumers, and how a pilot informed the final design hosted online.
A figure caption for lymph node tissue results, introducing the risk of bias summary for pleural TB in pleural fluid.

Tabulates the attributes and levels used in the provider and consumer choice experiments, such as cost, time to results, need for follow-up visits, false positive and negative rates, testing location and how the test is done.

Describes recruitment of choice experiment participants through TB networks and WHO groups, the online consent process and analysis methods. It summarizes respondents, most of whom were based in India, the United States, South Africa, Pakistan and Zimbabwe.
Tabulates characteristics of the 186 provider and 48 consumer respondents and begins the choice analysis, noting that consumers strongly preferred any test over no test.

Reports that for providers, after accuracy, the most influential attributes were avoiding an in-person follow-up visit and not needing specialist staff or equipment, with cost least important. It presents the model results and notes that providers valued avoiding follow-up far more than consumers did.
Shows how much higher false-positive rate consumers and providers would accept in exchange for other test attributes, such as avoiding a seven-day wait for results.

Summarizes the choice experiment: consumers most preferred testing in primary care rather than hospitals, and both groups would accept lower accuracy to get faster results and avoid follow-up visits. It notes that too few responses were collected to compare preferences across regions.

Introduces the report on user perspectives on TB infection testing, describing TB's global burden and that about a quarter to a third of people are estimated to have TB infection, which can progress to disease. It describes current tests (TST and IGRA) and the newer antigen-based skin tests, which are portable and expected to be low cost but need two clinic visits.

Explains that WHO commissioned reviews of user perspectives on the new skin tests because their acceptability, feasibility and equity effects were unknown. It outlines the three work packages, a systematic review, user interviews and a discrete choice experiment, guided by an expert advisory panel.

Introduces Work Package A, two systematic reviews of qualitative evidence on end users' views of antigen-based skin tests compared with IGRA and TST, and on their equity effects. It describes the database searches, including Russian and Chinese databases and a WHO public call for data.

Sets out the review eligibility criteria, which required qualitative data collection and analysis, and describes screening in duplicate, including by native speakers for Russian and Chinese database results.

Reports Xpert Ultra accuracy for pleural TB in pleural fluid, with 74.0% sensitivity and 88.1% specificity from 13 studies against a microbiological reference. It also gives estimates against a composite reference and introduces results for pleural tissue.
Describes data extraction in duplicate using Covidence, the study characteristics recorded, and the use of GRADE-CERQual to rate confidence in each review finding.
Reports that four studies met the inclusion criteria: one on a skin test from WHO's call for data and three on IGRA and TST, published between 2014 and 2021, with PRISMA flow charts.

Describes the included studies, including the only skin test study on Diaskintest in a mass screening programme for children in the Russian Federation, and three studies on IGRA and TST. It begins describing the confidence ratings for the review findings.
Reports that findings on values, acceptability and feasibility were rated moderate confidence and health equity low, owing to few studies, thin data and focus on specific subgroups.
Tabulates the characteristics of the four included studies, including test, country, setting, participants, methods, conceptual framework and conflicts of interest.

Presents review findings on end-user values and acceptability, combining both reviews because data were scarce. It notes the perceived accuracy of the tests and that clinic staff had concerns about IGRA accuracy in adults with HIV.

Continues the findings on acceptability, noting that perceived IGRA indeterminate results were not borne out by clinic data, and that convenience shaped test preferences in all four studies. Quotes illustrate views on human error in skin tests and discomfort from the TST.

Describes test-related factors in acceptability, with skin tests and IGRA seen as more specific than the TST, which had many false positives. It notes that the skin test's specificity encouraged parents to have children tested, and that no study assessed TBST feasibility, with moderate confidence in the evidence.

Describes individual factors in feasibility, especially the TST's need for a return visit within 72 hours, which was hard for people facing long journeys, waits and transport problems in South Africa and the United States. It reports that using routine blood draws for IGRA was seen as easing logistics.

Reports concern that linking TB testing to infrequent CD4 blood draws might delay diagnosis, and providers' view that it could complement rather than replace other testing. It summarizes contextual feasibility factors such as transport, waiting times, scalability and suitability for subgroups.

Reports that two studies on pleural tissue showed sensitivities of 80–100% and specificities of 75–86% against a microbiological reference, with low or very low certainty. It also covers composite reference results and introduces genitourinary TB in urine.

Describes access and transport as the main equity issue, with the TST return visit a barrier in several studies, alongside shortages of trained staff. It notes reports that Diaskintest worked well for mass screening of children.

Summarizes Work Package A: only four studies were found, mostly on TST and IGRA in specific settings, limiting confidence, but key factors for values, acceptability, feasibility and equity were identified and used to shape the interviews and choice experiment.

Introduces Work Package B, a qualitative interview study with 20 people living with TB or providers involved in TB testing and care, recruited through global networks with WHO support. It lists the recruiting organizations and the objectives on views of skin tests and equity.
Lists the topics covered in the interviews, from current use of skin tests to user preferences, feasibility, acceptability and equity, and summarizes participants' roles and countries.

Explains that the interview analysis used the same people, test and context subthemes as the reviews, and begins reporting findings on end-user values, such as the hope that more accurate tests would reduce unnecessary treatment and stress.

Reports that interviewees saw the TST as less accurate, leading to costly and stressful follow-up after false positives. It also describes the resources each test requires, with IGRA needing laboratories, phlebotomy and trained staff.

Notes that skin tests need less infrastructure than IGRA, then sets out seven people-related factors affecting acceptability, such as consumer experience, perceptions, knowledge and provider communication. It describes anxiety linked to new tests, injections and uncertain skin reactions.

Presents interview findings on the patient experience of tuberculosis infection tests, with quotes on initial fear of injections and the reassurance of seeing the result on one's own arm. A provider describes how long it took to convince people that skin testing was safe. Other participants compare skin tests with blood draws, one noting local myths about taking blood.

Reports that the complex steps of skin testing, such as avoiding rubbing the site and returning for a reading, may reduce acceptability for people with low health literacy. It notes concerns about using blood tests and skin tests in people with darker skin, where veins and reactions can be harder to see. Some providers questioned continuing with skin tests at all.

Continues with a provider's view that skin testing is outdated technology, then reports that most participants knew little about the novel skin tests and wanted evidence and public awareness. Familiarity with existing skin tests and endorsement by bodies such as WHO were expected to improve acceptance.

Reports that Xpert Ultra on urine had 100% sensitivity in three studies but widely varying specificity against a microbiological reference, with low sensitivity against a composite reference. It introduces results for bone or joint TB.

Reports that some consumers doubted the usefulness of the novel skin tests without proof they beat existing tests or without follow-up care after a positive result. It introduces test factors affecting acceptability, with providers favouring novel skin tests over the tuberculin skin test for better specificity.

Includes a provider's criticism of how hard it is to measure induration precisely, then lists perceived downstream benefits of more accurate novel tests, such as fewer false positives, better diagnosis and avoiding unnecessary treatment. It notes that none of the three test types can distinguish latent from active tuberculosis.

Quotes a provider on the difficulty of finding a biomarker to separate latent and active tuberculosis, then describes contextual factors in acceptability: provider perceptions, follow-up infrastructure and the test environment. Only consumers raised the test environment as a factor.

Begins the feasibility findings, noting that consumer experience was the only people-related factor discussed and that IGRA's single visit was seen by some providers as an advantage over skin tests needing a return visit.

Quotes providers on the advantage of IGRA needing no return visit and describes the transport and parking burden of attending hospital for a blood test, likely greater in lower-income countries. It then notes that skin tests were seen as cheaper than IGRA.

Reports that providers saw cost savings from novel skin tests and thought low cost might make governments more willing to fund them, especially where sputum collection from children is difficult. It then discusses ease of administration, with the tuberculin skin test seen as manageable with trained staff.

Presents provider views that the tuberculin skin test is fiddly at first but easy with practice, though staff may need frequent retraining. It notes judgements on the ease of novel skin tests and introduces contextual feasibility factors: resource needs, the COVID-19 pandemic and the health system setting.

Explains that all three test types need equipment and trained staff, but IGRA also needs a laboratory, a blood draw and patient travel, making it less feasible in resource-limited settings. It introduces equity factors, noting tests needing less infrastructure were seen as more accessible.

Describes how portable skin tests can reach people far from health facilities, avoiding travel, crowded clinics and long waits, an advantage in low-resource settings. It notes IGRA was seen as less suited to low-income countries because of cost and resource needs.

Presents quotes on making testing more affordable where tuberculosis burden is high and phlebotomy is unavailable, and on the scalability of skin tests for large screening in hard-to-reach communities. It concludes that equity impacts may vary by population group.

Reports Xpert Ultra accuracy for bone or joint TB, with 96.6% sensitivity and 91.1% specificity from three studies against a microbiological reference. A single study against a composite reference gave 90% sensitivity and 97% specificity.

Summarises interview findings that providers and consumers value accuracy, convenience, good patient experience, low cost and low resource needs. Novel skin tests were seen as similar in accuracy to IGRA but cheaper and less resource-intensive, and more accurate than the tuberculin skin test, though still needing a return visit. It adds that wider access barriers in low-income settings will not be solved by introducing the new tests alone.

Concludes that novel skin tests were judged more acceptable than and as feasible as the tuberculin skin test, with greater equity benefits, while IGRA remains preferred in well-resourced high-income settings.

Introduces Work Package C, a discrete choice experiment to explore how test users and providers trade off test attributes. It describes the online cross-sectional survey design and how attributes covering acceptability, accuracy, feasibility and equity were chosen.

Explains how choice tasks offered two hypothetical tests plus an opt-out, with separate versions for providers and consumers, and how a 10-task efficient design was built from the many possible profiles using NGENE software after piloting.

Sets out limitations of the choice experiment, including possible hypothetical bias, recruitment of only about a quarter of the target consumer sample, and too few responses to explore differences between geographic settings.

The opening of the executive summary on targeted next-generation sequencing for TB drug susceptibility testing, explaining that current rapid tests detect resistance to few drugs. It describes the review's objective and the use of individual-level data from several studies. It outlines the modelling approach, including covariables such as Xpert semi-quantitative results and rifampicin resistance.

Continues the description of methods, including the use of HIV data from FIND and how study sites were handled, and reports rifampicin resistance results. It notes that phenotypic testing misses borderline resistance, so a composite reference standard is preferred for rifampicin.

Reports pooled accuracy of targeted sequencing for isoniazid resistance, at 96% sensitivity and 97% specificity, and for levofloxacin, moxifloxacin and pyrazinamide. Each result gives the number of studies, indeterminate rates, certainty of evidence and expected results per 1000 patients.

Reports pooled targeted sequencing accuracy for ethambutol against composite and phenotypic standards, and repeats results for isoniazid and fluoroquinolones. Each result gives the certainty of evidence and the expected true and false results per 1000 patients.

Reports targeted sequencing accuracy for pyrazinamide, with 90% sensitivity and 99% specificity against a composite standard. It then covers bedaquiline, linezolid and clofazimine against phenotypic testing, giving expected results per 1000 patients.
Reports targeted sequencing accuracy for amikacin, ethambutol and streptomycin, and summarises that indeterminate rates were mostly around 10-20%. It leads into the authors' conclusions.

Concludes that the impact of targeted sequencing depends on where it is placed, with stronger evidence for reflex testing after rifampicin resistance is found than as an initial test, and calls for studies on extrapulmonary specimens.

Sets out the background to a WHO-commissioned review of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) for detecting drug resistance in tuberculosis, explaining that empirical treatment risks failure and amplified resistance where resistance is common. It notes that phenotypic drug susceptibility testing remains out of reach for most patients and that molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF, line-probe assays and Xpert XDR cover only some drugs. It argues that new regimens such as BPaLM have outpaced companion diagnostics and that sequencing directly from samples could help protect these drugs.

Describes the clinical pathway assessed, first testing tNGS for first-line drugs and fluoroquinolones in all TB patients and then for other drugs in rifampicin-resistant patients, with sub-analyses by Xpert bacterial load and HIV status. It explains the four possible test outcomes, true and false positives and negatives, and their consequences for patient treatment. It also notes that Deeplex Myc-TB can report uncharacterized mutations, which the review counts with failures as indeterminate results; some quoted terms on the page have missing letters in the extracted text.

Sets out the review's two questions: whether tNGS should be the first test for drug resistance in bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB, and whether it should be used for patients with rifampicin-resistant TB, listing the drugs and reference standards for each. It states the review objective and notes sub-analyses for people with HIV and low bacterial load as a proxy for children.

Describes the methods, including prospective clinical studies testing tNGS directly on samples, phenotypic DST as the reference and composite references with whole genome sequencing for rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide. It lists the drugs assessed and gives the database search strategy, run in 2022 and repeated in 2023, with independent screening by two reviewers.

Lists inclusion criteria, such as specific tNGS platforms, bacteriologically confirmed TB, an accepted reference standard and available individual patient data, and explains the decision to run only an individual patient data meta-analysis. It then begins describing the QUADAS-2 quality assessment, starting with patient selection.

Continues the QUADAS-2 assessment for the index test, reference standard and flow and timing, noting that some operators misread Deeplex Myc-TB's uncharacterized variant calls. It then introduces GRADE grading of the certainty of evidence.

Explains the GRADE rules applied, such as downgrading for indirectness when studies were enriched for rifampicin resistance and for imprecision when confidence intervals were wide. It describes the statistical analysis, including minimum sample numbers per platform and drug and rules for excluding weaker platforms to support a class-based recommendation.

Explains why an individual patient data meta-analysis was used, citing small studies, the ability to include covariates and repeated testing of the same samples on several platforms. It describes building mixed-effects models for sensitivity, specificity and predictive values with covariates such as Xpert rifampicin result, bacterial load and HIV status.

Explains that, for FIND data, the repeat Xpert result informed the reference standard while the screening result was used as a model covariate, reflecting the likely real-world use of tNGS as a follow-on test after Xpert.

Reports the search results, with 876 articles screened and four published studies included from Germany, India and France, describing their settings and sample processing. It introduces unpublished data, the largest being a FIND head-to-head study of Deeplex Myc-TB and NanoTB in South Africa, India and Georgia.

Describes further unpublished data sources, including the DIAMA study in six African countries, studies in Bangladesh, South Africa and Italy, and notes which sources provided Xpert rifampicin and semi-quantitative results.

Presents the flow chart of studies and explains that no drugs were dropped, while up to two platforms per drug were excluded for too few samples or performance well below the best platform, as shown in Table 1.

Presents Table 1, giving resistant and susceptible sample numbers and raw sensitivity and specificity of the Deeplex, NanoTB and TBSeq platforms for each drug. It shows high sensitivity for most drugs but low values for some platforms with bedaquiline, clofazimine and linezolid.
Lists, in Table 2, the number of samples from each platform included in the meta-analysis for each drug, with a figure on data sources.

Summarises the meta-analysis results, with sensitivity above 85% for all drugs except bedaquiline, linezolid and clofazimine (around 68–70%) and specificity above 90% except for streptomycin and for rifampicin against phenotypic DST alone. Table 3 gives pooled sensitivity, specificity and predictive values for each drug under both review questions.

Presents Table 4 with sub-analysis results by Xpert bacterial load and HIV status for isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide, showing true and false results, sensitivity, specificity and indeterminate rates. Indeterminate results were much more common in low-load and HIV-positive samples.

Continues Table 4 for pyrazinamide, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, amikacin, streptomycin and the newer drugs, showing accuracy by bacterial load and HIV status and higher indeterminate rates in low-load samples. Footnotes flag where models could not control for certain covariates. For linezolid, very few resistant samples were available in the sub-groups.

Explains how the detailed results for each question are presented and reports that, for rifampicin against a composite reference, nine studies gave pooled sensitivity of 93% and specificity of 96%. Evidence was rated moderate for sensitivity and low for specificity after downgrading for indirectness and imprecision.

Reports pooled sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 81% for rifampicin against phenotypic DST, with certainty rated moderate for sensitivity and very low for specificity.

Reports that tNGS as the initial test for isoniazid resistance had pooled sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 97%, based on twelve studies. Certainty was rated moderate for both after downgrading for indirectness.

Reports pooled sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 96% for levofloxacin, with certainty rated low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity.
Reports that tNGS as the initial test for moxifloxacin resistance had pooled sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 96%, with certainty rated moderate for both.
Introduces the analysis of tNGS for pyrazinamide resistance against a composite reference, reporting pooled sensitivity of 88%.
Reports pooled specificity of 99% for pyrazinamide against the composite reference, with certainty rated moderate for both sensitivity and specificity.

Reports that tNGS for pyrazinamide resistance against phenotypic DST had pooled sensitivity of 85% and specificity of 94%. Certainty was rated low for sensitivity, because a Bangladesh study was an outlier, and moderate for specificity.

Reports that tNGS for ethambutol resistance against a composite reference had pooled sensitivity of 96% and very high specificity and positive predictive value. It notes the model could not control for rifampicin resistance because of collinearity.

Explains the GRADE judgement for ethambutol against the composite reference, rated low for both sensitivity and specificity because different samples were used for index and reference tests and studies were enriched for rifampicin resistance.

Reports that tNGS for ethambutol resistance against phenotypic DST, based on a single study, had pooled sensitivity of 88%. Certainty was rated very low for both sensitivity and specificity because of risk of bias, enrichment and reliance on one study.

Introduces the analysis of tNGS for moxifloxacin resistance in rifampicin-resistant TB, with sample numbers, resistance prevalence and indeterminate rate.
Reports pooled sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 95% for moxifloxacin in rifampicin-resistant TB, with high certainty for both.
Reports that tNGS for pyrazinamide resistance against a composite reference in rifampicin-resistant TB had high accuracy, with specificity of 99% and high certainty for both measures.

Summarises the economic review, which searched three databases in 2022 and included ten studies on tNGS and whole genome sequencing for drug-resistant TB, finding tNGS costs of about US$70 per sample and wider ranges for whole genome sequencing. It identifies sequencing as the costliest step, reagents and consumables as the main cost components and drivers such as sequencer choice, coverage depth and batching, and calls for more cost-effectiveness research.

Introduces the economic review, citing WHO estimates of 10.6 million TB cases and 1.6 million deaths in 2021 and defining forms of drug-resistant TB from rifampicin-resistant to extensively drug-resistant. It notes that resistance is concentrated in some high-burden countries and regions. It then explains that conventional phenotypic testing is slow and needs high-level biosafety laboratories and skilled staff.

Describes line-probe assays as faster molecular alternatives with limits for pre-XDR, XDR and extrapulmonary TB, and explains next-generation sequencing approaches, including whole genome sequencing, tNGS and metagenomics, and their workflow steps. It then begins the methods, noting the review followed PRISMA guidelines with a librarian-supported search strategy.

Describes the search and eligibility methods of systematic and scoping reviews on the costs of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) for diagnosing drug-resistant TB. It lists the databases searched in October 2022, the inclusion of studies on confirmed or suspected DR-TB, and the cost outcomes of interest such as cost per sample, component costs, costs per step and ICERs.

Explains that heterogeneity ruled out meta-analysis, so a narrative synthesis was done with costs converted to 2021 US dollars, and that study quality was rated with a modified CHEERS checklist. It then describes which cost measures the included tNGS and WGS studies reported and notes that few costed the phenotypic comparator.

Summarizes six studies reporting tNGS costs for drug-resistant TB, their settings and whether testing was on site or centralized. It reports the limited data on cost per sample and the wide range in sequencer prices, from about $1 000 for a Nanopore MinION to over $200 000 for an Illumina NextSeq.

Reports per-sample reagent and consumable costs for different tNGS platforms, which varied widely by manufacturer and workflow. It then presents a five-year budget impact analysis comparing tNGS, WGS and phenotypic testing scenarios, with start-up costs in the first year driven by equipment.

Notes the extra first-year start-up costs in the budget scenarios and points to an appendix for WGS results. Continues the scoping review findings on sequencing costs for diseases such as HIV, covering component costs, sequencer capital costs and costs per step. It lists factors that influence costs, such as laboratory efficiency, staff, technology and volume discounts, and begins the quality assessment.

Gives quality scores for the scoping review studies and opens the discussion, describing the systematic review as the first on tNGS economics for drug-resistant TB and noting the scarcity of data. It discusses why per-sample costs vary, including platform choice, coverage depth and early-run inefficiencies reported in one study.

Adds that low sample volumes and limited batching raise per-sample sequencing costs. It then interprets the scoping review, highlighting a modelling study in which molecular testing plus WGS was the most cost-effective TB diagnostic strategy owing to greater sensitivity and faster diagnosis.

Concludes that more research is needed on cost-effectiveness, cost drivers such as batching and multiplexing, and full costing including overheads before tNGS and WGS economics for drug-resistant TB are well understood. It introduces the PRISMA flow diagram for the systematic review.
