The title page of Web Annex B.18, a 2023 report on stakeholder experiences of using targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) to diagnose MDR-TB, naming the author and the WHO unit it was prepared for.

The abstract explains that tNGS on sputum can diagnose drug-resistant TB within days instead of weeks, but faces implementation barriers. It states that interviews with implementers aimed to inform a new WHO guideline by exploring acceptability, feasibility, values, preferences and equity. It begins reporting that implementers saw the technology as a major advance but found platforms complex, with few chances to catch errors early.

Continues the abstract's findings on tNGS feasibility, including specialized laboratories and staff found only in central facilities and needs for stable power, internet, computing, clean water and temperature control. It also notes supply chain delays and data management concerns. Turning to values and equity, participants worried about the cost of equipment, reagents and maintenance and called for comprehensive costing.

Finishes the abstract's findings, calling for full cost-effectiveness analysis, synergies within diagnostic algorithms and stronger laboratory and health systems, including clinician training. It concludes that adoption in low- and middle-income countries should weigh ease of use, organizational context and stakeholder values as well as effectiveness.

Gives background on MDR-TB, noting that only about two in three cases are diagnosed and most patients are not cured, partly because of diagnostic and treatment delays. It explains that culture-based drug susceptibility testing takes weeks and that the End TB Strategy calls for universal testing. It then describes the tNGS workflow, stressing the precise library preparation needed before sequencing.

Completes the description of the tNGS workflow and notes known barriers to rapid diagnostics, such as cost, workflow integration, training and interpreting sequence data. It explains why health worker perspectives on implementability matter. It restates the study's objective of informing WHO guidance on tNGS.

Describes the qualitative methods, using semi-structured interviews with implementers of the FIND trial in reference laboratories in Georgia, India and South Africa, plus coordinators and other global sites. It explains purposive selection of staff with hands-on experience. It also describes recording, verbatim quotes and interview summaries as the main data source.

Explains that participants checked interview summaries, which were analysed thematically under acceptability, feasibility, and values, preferences and equity. It notes confidentiality agreements, so countries are anonymized as A, B and C. Findings begin with strong acceptability because tNGS is comprehensive, uses sputum and is fast.

Reports that all participants saw tNGS as a major advance, with results in 3–5 days rather than 4–6 weeks and testing for more drugs, including new and repurposed ones. Quotes describe it as revolutionary while noting it is still evolving. Participants felt now is the time to build expertise before resistance to newer drugs rises.

Reports the overall view that tNGS needs further development before routine use. It lists challenges such as start-up problems, specialized staff and laboratories, supply chains, complex library preparation, data management and security, and the need to keep the WHO mutation catalogue updated. It begins describing how skilled molecular scientists were available only at central laboratories.

Explains that tNGS required highly trained molecular scientists found only in reference laboratories, so it could not be decentralized. Quotes say routine technicians could not run the test in its current form and that automation would help. It also describes requirements for high-capacity computers and internet access for data analysis.

Describes the reliance of tNGS platforms on stable, high-capacity internet for uploading large data files. It reports supply chain disruptions, with specialist kits ordered from overseas causing delays. It also describes the demanding precision of sample and library preparation and the need to avoid cross-contamination.

Describes problems implementers faced, such as contaminated controls, data upload and software problems, temperature sensitivity and failed runs eventually traced to water quality. Participants called for simplifying the many library preparation steps so that less specialized staff could perform them. It notes that the trial stopped at producing reports, so clinicians' use of results was not evaluated.

Describes tNGS reports, which give resistance or susceptibility for each drug with a confidence level based on the WHO mutation catalogue, plus lineage data useful for surveillance. Participants noted uncertainty about resistance to newer drugs such as bedaquiline. They called the WHO catalogue essential and wanted automatic links between tNGS software and laboratory information systems.

Compares feasibility views across platforms, with library preparation seen as more complex for Deeplex than for Oxford Nanopore. Both were thought to lack early error detection, risking wasted runs. Quotes describe the products as immature and not yet market-ready.

Lists areas for future tNGS development, such as reducing complexity, automating links to data analysis, securing supplies and local technical support. Participants wanted a lower-complexity platform, for example with robotic liquid handling, so testing could be decentralized. Some hoped for point-of-care tests close to patients.

Discusses equitable access, noting that placing tNGS only in reference laboratories may disadvantage some regions and that batching in low-caseload settings causes delays. A participant called for 'plug and play' single-sample testing at affordable cost. It begins listing the costs that comprehensive costing should include, such as computing and storage.

Adds that costing should include maintenance, internet capacity and links to laboratory information systems. Participants argued cost-effectiveness should reflect accuracy, indeterminate results and impact on treatment outcomes, accepting short delays for reliable results. A participant hoped tNGS would replace rather than add to existing tests.

Discusses how tNGS fits a shift from phenotypic to genotypic testing and the cost of needing both. A participant called for a simple molecular technology to manage most patients quickly, leaving complex cases for further testing. Others stressed that rapid diagnostics only pay off if laboratories and health systems become more efficient.

Quotes a global expert who argued that time gained in the laboratory is lost if the health system cannot find and treat patients. It calls for better sample referral, communication between clinicians and laboratories and clinician training on using results. A summary table of findings begins with acceptability.

Continues the summary of findings, listing feasibility challenges and values, preferences and equity considerations such as placement, affordability, algorithm synergies and health system strengthening. It begins the discussion, noting the positive views alongside concerns about centralization, cost and equitable access.

Discusses participants' wish for affordable, automated point-of-care MDR-TB diagnostics and caution about integrating new tests. It notes that some feasibility challenges, such as supply chains and support, may persist and that the findings echo the 2018 WHO guidance on tNGS. It calls for evaluations of impact on treatment outcomes and mixed-methods research including providers and patients.

Closes the discussion of a primary qualitative study on implementing targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) for MDR-TB diagnosis, calling for policy support to strengthen laboratory and health system functions. It sets out strengths, such as being the first study of tNGS implementers and interviewing them soon after the FIND trial, and limitations, such as limited depth across several groups and uncertainty over which problems stem from the technology being new. It concludes that tNGS is seen as a major advance but needs further development, and introduces considerations for manufacturers and decision-makers.

Lists considerations for implementing tNGS in low- and middle-income countries, including advance planning for equipment procurement and customs clearance, hands-on training, troubleshooting and consumables checklists and local vendor support. It also calls for specialist molecular staff and for platforms to be made field-ready with simpler sample preparation.

Continues the considerations, calling for more automation, seamless links between sequencing and data analysis, data storage, ownership and security arrangements and interoperability with laboratory information systems. It also stresses affordability, sustainable funding and full costing, and concludes that guidelines should consider ease of use, organizational context and stakeholder values as well as effectiveness.

Credits the study's lead author, thanks interview participants, experts and WHO staff, and states no conflicts of interest, before beginning the reference list. The references include work on drug-resistant TB and on health workers and policy implementation in South Africa.

Ends the reference list and presents the interview guide for laboratory staff and managers at trial sites, with questions on their roles, experience with molecular and sequencing technologies and preparatory work for tNGS. It then moves on to their experiences across sample and library preparation.

Continues the interview guide with questions on what worked well or poorly in sequencing and data analysis, how tNGS compares with other drug-resistance tests and what enabling factors would help it improve TB care. It closes with contact details for the researcher.

Presents the information and consent form for the interview study on tNGS for detecting TB drug resistance, explaining its purpose of informing WHO guidance by exploring acceptability, feasibility, equity, values and preferences at FIND trial sites and elsewhere. It describes the independent researcher, procedures, confidentiality and the absence of expected benefits or harms.

The title page of Web Annex B.19, a qualitative evidence synthesis by Natalie Leon on stakeholder experiences of using tNGS to diagnose MDR-TB, dated 2022–2023 and prepared for WHO's TB unit.

The abstract of the qualitative evidence synthesis, explaining that tNGS can give comprehensive drug-resistance results within days but faces technical, organizational and economic barriers. It describes a rapid review that searched Medline and other sources in 2022, with single-reviewer screening and planned thematic synthesis and CERQual assessment. It reports that no eligible studies were found and points to the companion primary study and a 2022 Cochrane review of other rapid TB tests as indirect evidence.

Concludes the abstract by noting the Cochrane review's attention to patient obstacles and calling for more qualitative research alongside tNGS trials and roll-out. The background describes TB and drug resistance as major threats and explains how tNGS works on sputum samples to report resistance to multiple drugs. It notes that some platforms also report lineage information useful for tracking resistant strains.

Describes the general tNGS workflow from sample preparation and DNA extraction under biosafety level 3 to library preparation, sequencing and data analysis, stressing its complexity. It notes the lack of evidence on implementation experiences. It explains that a separate primary qualitative study was carried out alongside the FIND trial in India, Georgia and South Africa.

States the review objective of synthesising qualitative evidence on acceptability, feasibility, values, preferences and equity of tNGS from health workers' perspectives. It describes the rapid review design and the inclusion and exclusion criteria, focusing on implementers but open to other stakeholders.

Describes the search methods, combining a Medline search run in August and October 2022 with open searching, hand searching and contacting experts, and single-author screening with WHO consultation. It reports that no eligible studies were found, mostly because papers were quantitative, discussion pieces or based on hypothetical views.

Discusses the empty review, noting that tNGS is not yet widely operational and that future effectiveness studies offer chances to study implementers' experiences. It recommends including qualitative process evaluations and draws on a Cochrane review of other rapid TB diagnostics that highlights implementation factors. It also notes that patients' experiences of rapid TB diagnostics are understudied.

Discusses strengths and limitations, noting that the empty result confirms a research gap and that the review used multiple search methods but rapid-review shortcuts such as single-reviewer screening. It closes with acknowledgements and a statement of no conflicts of interest.

The title page of Web Annex B.20, a systematic review and meta-analysis of the accuracy of Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests, listing the review team and advisers and noting it was prepared for a February 2022 WHO guideline meeting.

The executive summary of the skin test review, explaining that new TB antigen-based skin tests could improve access to TB infection testing if as accurate as IGRA and the tuberculin skin test. It describes updating an earlier review with searches of English, Russian and Chinese databases to July 2021, random-effects meta-analyses, a post-hoc pooled analysis requested by WHO for a class-based recommendation, and notes that no longitudinal studies were found.

Reports that C-Tb studies came from South Africa, Spain and the UK, Diaskintest studies almost all from Russia and C-TST studies from China, and that Diaskintest studies had high risk of bias. It summarises sensitivity results showing Diaskintest, the tuberculin skin test and IGRAs performed similarly in adults with active TB, C-Tb had similar sensitivity to comparators, and agreement with IGRA was generally higher than with the skin test.

Reports further agreement results, such as about 95% agreement of Diaskintest with IGRA and highly variable agreement with the tuberculin skin test in children, and agreement of C-Tb with IGRA and the skin test in various groups. It notes limitations such as few responses from authors, and concludes that the new skin tests perform broadly like IGRA.

Completes the conclusion, noting variable Diaskintest results likely due to observational designs and BCG vaccination and better data for C-Tb and C-TST, with more research needed. The background explains that about a quarter of the world's population has TB infection with a 5–10% lifetime risk of disease. It argues that current infection tests are imperfect and that new skin tests may perform well in children and people with HIV.

Notes that the earlier review found new skin tests performed similarly to the tuberculin skin test and IGRA, and explains the hierarchy of reference standards used because no gold standard exists for TB infection. It sets out the review aim and begins a table of populations, tests, comparators and outcomes.

Completes the table of review questions, covering at-risk populations, BCG status and outcomes such as concordance with other tests and proportion started on preventive treatment. It begins the methods, setting out inclusion and exclusion criteria for study designs.

Tabulates inclusion criteria by objective, such as longitudinal studies of incident TB, contact studies by proximity, and studies of confirmed TB or low-risk groups for sensitivity and specificity. It describes the search, including Russian, Ukrainian and Chinese sources screened by native speakers or translation.

Describes resolving screening disagreements, using Rayyan and Excel for data management, and case definitions for incident, prevalent and active TB. It explains quality assessment with QUADAS-2, with an added domain on manufacturer involvement.

Explains use of GRADE and the analysis plan, including sensitivity in confirmed TB, specificity in low-risk groups in low-burden countries, test agreement with exact confidence intervals and meta-analysis where two or more studies existed. It sets out less restrictive proxy measures of specificity, restricted to presumed healthy people.

Explains that proxy specificity also included people with other diseases and that publication bias was not tested because of too few studies. It notes that, at WHO's request, data across different skin tests were pooled post hoc despite heterogeneity and high risk of bias in Diaskintest studies.

Presents Table 4, listing the effect measures for each review objective, such as incidence rate ratios and predictive values for progression, odds ratios by contact proximity, sensitivity and specificity, concordance and the proportion starting preventive treatment.

Reports the study selection, with the earlier review's 37 studies and new reports bringing totals to five C-Tb, 34 Diaskintest, four C-TST and one DPPD study, noting that DPPD data are shown but not pooled.

The title page of Web Annex B21, a systematic review and meta-analysis on the safety of tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests, naming the review team and advisers and noting it was prepared for a WHO guideline meeting in February 2022.
The list of abbreviations used in the safety review of novel tuberculosis skin tests.

The executive summary of the safety review explains that the tuberculin skin test is known to be safe but that newer antigen-based skin tests had not been systematically assessed. It describes searches of English, Russian and Chinese databases up to July 2021, plus manufacturer data and a WHO call for data. It notes that some studies were at high risk of bias owing to lack of blinding or passive collection of adverse events.

Summarises key findings: injection site reactions with C-Tb were no more common than with TST and were mostly mild or moderate, while one Chinese report found more reactions with C-TST. Diaskintest safety data were too inconsistent to pool, and overall no safety signal was seen that would affect the choice between the novel tests and TST. The background notes that about a quarter of the world's population has tuberculosis infection.

Explains why better tests for tuberculosis infection are needed, describing the drawbacks of TST, such as false positives after BCG vaccination, low sensitivity in people with HIV and the need for two visits. It notes that the safety of the novel skin tests had not previously been reviewed and states the review's objective.

Sets out the review's aim and PICO question on whether novel skin tests cause more adverse reactions than TST or IGRA, the outcomes sought, and inclusion criteria naming the index tests, such as C-Tb, Diaskintest and C-TST, and comparators.

Explains how adverse reactions were defined, noting that induration is the intended response and counting only exaggerated reactions as adverse where trials did so. Severity was graded with the DAIDS scale and serious events defined in standard terms, followed by exclusion criteria and the search strategy.

Describes how studies in English, Russian and Chinese were screened and data extracted by pairs of independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by discussion. It explains how risk of bias was judged for randomised and non-randomised studies.

Describes the use of GRADE and the statistical methods, including random-effects meta-analysis of risk ratios and pooled proportions and combining trial and observational data where appropriate. It begins describing the included studies, which covered several recombinant antigen preparations.

Notes that no safety data were found for DPPD and that the report focuses on C-Tb, C-TST and Diaskintest. It describes the seven C-Tb studies, five of which were double-blind comparisons with TST at low risk of bias, though systemic events could not be attributed to one test when both were given.

Describes the C-TST studies, all in HIV-negative adults in China, which were non-blinded and at serious risk of bias for outcome measurement. It notes that most Diaskintest studies collected adverse events passively and poorly defined them, placing them at high risk of bias.
